editions.intro:
Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned, and the shares jumped roughly 30 per cent. Nvidia fell almost 6 per cent on Tuesday, Anthropic slipped below its $83 IPO price, and investigators and Congress are still circling the company over alleged chip diversion to China.

The wider AI sell-off remains the bigger story for markets. The S&P 500 and Dow have entered correction after a seventh straight losing session, Asian markets had their steepest slide since 2020, and regulators in China, South Korea and Taiwan have introduced emergency measures. Washington's response has widened the story: the Commerce Department blacklisted Megaspeed and six Southeast Asian firms, Malaysia is working on new licensing curbs, and Alice Huang's alleged links to Chinese intelligence are drawing scrutiny of Lutnick and Bessent.

Elsewhere, the US is reportedly preparing new tariffs on at least 14 trading partners, the Huawei conviction in Brooklyn, and a Chinese anti-graft probe into Shanghai's party chief all add to a crowded news day. Climate talks in Antalya collapsed over fossil fuel language, and a Democratic House majority is set to take shape in Washington.

Behind the sell-off are worries about debt-funded AI spending. Nvidia's leadership is also in turmoil. Away from markets, Andy Burnham's UK-EU reset deals on trade, emissions and youth mobility are drawing fire, with student fees still unresolved. editions.intro:
Anthropic's record stock market debut dominated the day, raising about $81bn at $83 a share and opening at $111.50 on Nasdaq. The euphoria did not spread. US indices fell more than 2% and the S&P 500 has now dropped six days running, while Asian markets are heading for their worst week since 2020, with Taiwan down 16%. Investors appear to be weighing a huge new supply of AI equity against stretched valuations, and Nvidia's shares have been hit since Jensen Huang's resignation.

The Gulf conflict also escalated. Iran fired missiles and drones at US sites in Kuwait and Bahrain after US strikes near the Strait of Hormuz, the second exchange since a memorandum of understanding was signed last week. Houthi missiles damaged parts of Riyadh, including the kingdom's tallest tower, and oil and shipping risks rose again.

Diplomacy at the APEC summit in Shenzhen produced a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin, but little of substance. Nuclear arms control, Ukraine and AI were left open, and Putin ruled out a limited ceasefire after the Crimean Bridge was struck again. Nvidia's search for a new chief executive has reportedly reached Arm's Rene Haas, while the Bank of England, the IMF and the ECB all point to tighter money ahead.

Finance.title: AI rout pushes US indexes into correction; Nvidia rebounds on Huang return
Finance.notification: Wall Street slides into correction as AI shares sell off, then Nvidia's 31% rebound on Huang's return
Finance.summary:
Markets have swung sharply on the AI trade. The S&P 500 closed down 3.59% on Friday, its seventh straight losing session, pushing it into correction territory, while chipmakers led a drop that spilled into Asia, where Taiwan, Korea and Japan fell by around 5%. Anthropic's record IPO, which raised about $81bn, has been overshadowed as its shares slipped from their debut close.

The mood reversed on Monday when Nvidia jumped about 31% after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Asian shares rallied hard, but the gains faded by Tuesday, with Nvidia down around 5% and AMD sharply lower as Huang faces congressional questions next week and fresh tariff reports rattle investors.

Beyond tech, the Bank of Japan has signalled further rate normalisation into 2027, and Brent crude sits near a three-month low at about $89 as supply rises. European gas prices are climbing on a cold-snap forecast, and the UK's Ofgem is expected to announce a 26% rise in its price cap.

World.title: Democrats take a large House majority as Trump's term turns divided
World.notification: Democrats win their biggest House majority since 1992, setting up a divided Washington under Trump.
World.summary:
Democrats have won their largest US House majority since 1992, with CNN projecting about 259 seats. Republican Chuck Hubbard's rival Virginia Foxx conceded in North Carolina after a recount, and four races remain uncalled. Democrats also hold the Senate with 56 seats, so Donald Trump now faces divided government. Voters cited prices, the war with Iran and corruption, and Democrats plan a 100-day agenda on living costs, healthcare and immigration, plus oversight of the administration.

The result matters for markets because it limits Trump's room to pass fresh legislation, though his veto power remains. Investors will also weigh it alongside a new US tariff plan reportedly due on Wednesday, which could strain China and EU trade ties. Oversight of the immigration crackdown was also raised after an ICE arrest at Seattle airport drew condemnation from state officials.

Beyond Washington, the biggest global story is the collapse of COP31 talks in Antalya over fossil fuel wording, while Russia and NATO face a new flare-up after Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland. In the UK, Andy Burnham's EU reset deal keeps drawing fire from former prime ministers and opposition parties.

Tech.notification: Alice Huang probe widens as senators demand Lutnick and Bessent testify under oath over Nvidia chips.
Tech.summary:
The biggest tech story is the widening scandal around Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia affair. New reporting links her to Chinese intelligence and to alleged chip smuggling, with the New York Times citing about $3.6bn of Chinese state money tied to her family's companies. Senator John Kennedy wants Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to testify under oath, and Nvidia says it has stopped H200 shipments to China.

The affair is also shaping markets. Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive after a unanimous board vote, but shares fell almost 6% on Tuesday as the rally faded, and analysts say scrutiny from the FBI and Congress continues. Anthropic's record $81bn IPO has slipped below its $83 offer price, and emerging-market stocks are heading for a loss that would erase their 2026 gains as doubts over the AI trade spread across Asia.

Beyond the scandal, the sector is grappling with security and governance. Prosecutors allege a former OpenAI engineer secretly recorded executive meetings, and Huawei was convicted of fraud and trade-secret theft in a US trial, though it plans to appeal.

Fashion.notification: Paolo Bulgari, who steered the jewellery house into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged 89.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in luxury today is the death of Paolo Bulgari, aged 89, in Rome. His family called him the greatest jeweller of his time. He joined the family firm in 1960, became chairman in 1984 and oversaw its growth into watches, perfumes and accessories, including the coloured-gemstone pieces that helped define the house. The family sold its controlling stake to LVMH in 2011.

Elsewhere, the business of luxury stayed busy. Shein agreed to pay $100 million to settle US Federal Trade Commission claims over misleading marketing, reviews and sourcing, a case that signals closer US scrutiny of origin claims. Leadership and succession also featured. J.Crew's chief marketing officer Julia Collier is leaving, reportedly for Skims, and Dior hired Nicole Orofino from L'Oréal as head of innovation for communication. A FashionSights report argues that family succession will drive consolidation across fashion, with 30 of the 100 largest family-controlled companies facing a handover.

Tech.title: Nvidia chief Huang quits amid affair scandal
Tech.notification: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, wiping up to $601bn off the chipmaker's value in a day
Tech.summary:
Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker worth roughly $4 trillion. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of relationships with a woman US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security and with a direct report, and the shares fell as much as 14% in early trading.

The fallout is spreading across the sector. Democratic senators have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports, and reports say the Commerce Department stalled action against Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected of routing chips to China. Investors are now focused on Nvidia's third-quarter results on 17 November, the first without Huang, and on whether the AI boom's financing web, which Huang helped build, holds up.

Beyond Nvidia, the sector is under pressure from a broad tech sell-off, AI-linked concerns in US midterm politics, and a heavy pipeline of listings. Anthropic's S-1 filing shows revenue growing very fast, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though with much larger losses.

World.title: Nvidia chief Huang quits amid affair and spy claims
World.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years, and the AI trade is asking what comes next.
World.summary:
Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years leading the chipmaker, following admissions of affairs, one with a woman US intelligence has determined was a Chinese spy and one with a company executive who reports to him. Nvidia shares fell sharply, and the wider AI trade has been unsettled by fears that a new leader could scale back the company's financing of customers and slow the AI build-out.

The episode also reaches into Washington and Taipei. A Republican senator has called for Huang to go, the House chairman says Huang has agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, and Taiwan is examining the woman's visits. Chinese AI firms are reportedly rushing to secure Nvidia capacity in case US rules on remote chip access tighten. Analysts will watch governance and export-control moves closely.

Beyond the chip story, the wider news is dominated by the Middle East and Ukraine. Oil rebounded after Trump questioned the need for an Iran deal, while Witkoff and Kushner met Putin, who signalled no compromise. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties is dividing Westminster ahead of a Brussels summit.

Fashion.title: Burberry rebounds as Capri names new CEO
Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Tech.title: Nvidia chip scandal drives tech sell-off and scrutiny
Tech.notification: Alice Huang probe widens as senators demand Lutnick and Bessent testify under oath over Nvidia chips.
Tech.summary:
The biggest tech story is the widening scandal around Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia affair. New reporting links her to Chinese intelligence and to alleged chip smuggling, with the New York Times citing about $3.6bn of Chinese state money tied to her family's companies. Senator John Kennedy wants Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to testify under oath, and Nvidia says it has stopped H200 shipments to China.

The affair is also shaping markets. Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive after a unanimous board vote, but shares fell almost 6% on Tuesday as the rally faded, and analysts say scrutiny from the FBI and Congress continues. Anthropic's record $81bn IPO has slipped below its $83 offer price, and emerging-market stocks are heading for a loss that would erase their 2026 gains as doubts over the AI trade spread across Asia.

Beyond the scandal, the sector is grappling with security and governance. Prosecutors allege a former OpenAI engineer secretly recorded executive meetings, and Huawei was convicted of fraud and trade-secret theft in a US trial, though it plans to appeal.

highlights.label: Huawei
highlights.text: A Brooklyn jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud and trade-secret theft. Sentencing is set for September 2027 and Huawei plans to appeal.

highlights.label: OpenAI security
highlights.text: Prosecutors say ex-engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan hid a recorder in an executive room and likely captured OpenAI trade secrets. He has pleaded not guilty.

highlights.text: Amazon is buying Decart's AI optimisation technology and its founders in a deal reported at around $7.5bn, an asset purchase rather than a full takeover.

highlights.label: Meta Muse

highlights.label: Social media
highlights.text: A Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube liable for designing addictive platforms, awarding $6m in total. Both say they will appeal.

Finance.title: AI rout pushes US indexes into correction; Nvidia rebounds on Huang return
Finance.notification: Wall Street slides into correction as AI shares sell off, then Nvidia's 31% rebound on Huang's return
Finance.summary:
Markets have swung sharply on the AI trade. The S&P 500 closed down 3.59% on Friday, its seventh straight losing session, pushing it into correction territory, while chipmakers led a drop that spilled into Asia, where Taiwan, Korea and Japan fell by around 5%. Anthropic's record IPO, which raised about $81bn, has been overshadowed as its shares slipped from their debut close.

The mood reversed on Monday when Nvidia jumped about 31% after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Asian shares rallied hard, but the gains faded by Tuesday, with Nvidia down around 5% and AMD sharply lower as Huang faces congressional questions next week and fresh tariff reports rattle investors.

Beyond tech, the Bank of Japan has signalled further rate normalisation into 2027, and Brent crude sits near a three-month low at about $89 as supply rises. European gas prices are climbing on a cold-snap forecast, and the UK's Ofgem is expected to announce a 26% rise in its price cap.

World.title: Democrats take a large House majority as Trump's term turns divided
World.notification: Democrats win their biggest House majority since 1992, setting up a divided Washington under Trump.
World.summary:
Democrats have won their largest US House majority since 1992, with CNN projecting about 259 seats. Republican Chuck Hubbard's rival Virginia Foxx conceded in North Carolina after a recount, and four races remain uncalled. Democrats also hold the Senate with 56 seats, so Donald Trump now faces divided government. Voters cited prices, the war with Iran and corruption, and Democrats plan a 100-day agenda on living costs, healthcare and immigration, plus oversight of the administration.

The result matters for markets because it limits Trump's room to pass fresh legislation, though his veto power remains. Investors will also weigh it alongside a new US tariff plan reportedly due on Wednesday, which could strain China and EU trade ties. Oversight of the immigration crackdown was also raised after an ICE arrest at Seattle airport drew condemnation from state officials.

Beyond Washington, the biggest global story is the collapse of COP31 talks in Antalya over fossil fuel wording, while Russia and NATO face a new flare-up after Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland. In the UK, Andy Burnham's EU reset deal keeps drawing fire from former prime ministers and opposition parties.

Fashion.title: Bulgari patriarch Paolo Bulgari dies at 89
Fashion.notification: Paolo Bulgari, who steered the jewellery house into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged 89.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in luxury today is the death of Paolo Bulgari, aged 89, in Rome. His family called him the greatest jeweller of his time. He joined the family firm in 1960, became chairman in 1984 and oversaw its growth into watches, perfumes and accessories, including the coloured-gemstone pieces that helped define the house. The family sold its controlling stake to LVMH in 2011.

Elsewhere, the business of luxury stayed busy. Shein agreed to pay $100 million to settle US Federal Trade Commission claims over misleading marketing, reviews and sourcing, a case that signals closer US scrutiny of origin claims. Dior added Stray Kids' Hyunjin as a brand ambassador for beauty and Jonathan Anderson's collections, while Louis Vuitton is opening a three-storey experiential flagship in Hong Kong on 12 December.

Leadership and succession also featured. J.Crew's chief marketing officer Julia Collier is leaving, reportedly for Skims, and Dior hired Nicole Orofino from L'Oréal as head of innovation for communication. A FashionSights report argues that family succession will drive consolidation across fashion, with 30 of the 100 largest family-controlled companies facing a handover.
